text:
Musk to Texas Democrats: Our Success Came From Freedom, Not Your Favors

Elon Musk just slapped down a Wall Street Journal story claiming Texas Democrats plan to yank the "white-glove treatment" for SpaceX and Tesla now that they've flipped the state. He made it plain: the companies thrived here because the government stayed out of the way.

"SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government," Musk wrote.

He explained the practical reasons too. Factories need hands-on leadership. "And I need to be close to the factories, so that I can walk the floor in person. That’s why the first major SpaceX factory was in LA and first major Tesla factory was in SF Bay Area."

Then California turned hostile. "As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas."

This is the same pattern that hollowed out California's tech and manufacturing base. High taxes, endless rules, and politicians treating productive companies like piñatas drove the growth elsewhere. Texas offered the opposite: lower burdens, faster permitting, and room to build. Jobs followed. Investment followed. Rockets and cars got built instead of lawsuits.

Now the new Democratic leadership is signaling they want to change the deal. They talk about ending special treatment, scrutinizing land deals, slowing data centers, and reviewing incentives. Translation: they see a successful employer and reach for the regulatory toolbox. The same approach that chased SpaceX and Tesla out of California is being imported to Texas.

Musk is not asking for favors. He is stating the obvious. Companies locate where they can operate without constant extraction and interference. Texas gained by being less California. If Democrats reverse that, the next expansion, the next factory, the next launch complex will simply go somewhere else. Florida has already been mentioned. Other red states are open for business.

The left celebrates the blue wave as a rebuke to Musk's spending. What they are actually celebrating is the chance to punish the companies that create the jobs and tax base they want to spend. History shows how that ends. California wrote the playbook. Texas is now being invited to copy it.

text:
Tesla announcing the end of Cybertruck production in mid-2027 has honestly left a bad taste in my mouth.

I’ve dreamed of owning a Tesla since I first drove one in 2018. I finally made that happen in 2025, although my delivery experience was far from pleasant. Today, I own a 2026 Model Y Premium AWD, but the Cybertruck has always been what I REALLY wanted.

The problem? Every time I got closer to comfortably affording one, the price seemed to move further out of reach. Now we’re looking at over $92K, and production is coming to an end.

Could I buy one? Absolutely. I have enough in savings to pay cash. But just because you CAN afford something doesn’t mean it’s financially responsible to buy it.

So now I’m questioning what’s next.

I drive roughly 30 miles a day, and I rarely use FSD (Supervised) outside of road trips. While I enjoy my Model Y, its ground clearance leaves something to be desired, especially as an essential employee who needs to get to work during Connecticut snowstorms.

That leaves me considering three options:

Keep my current Model Y.
Upgrade to another Model Y Premium AWD with the tow package, larger 16-inch screen, and black headliner.
Leave Tesla and consider the Rivian R2, which offers the additional ground clearance I’m looking for.

And here’s the thing: I don’t necessarily need FSD (Supervised) or Autonomy+. They’re nice features, but I barely use them. Rivian’s technology will continue improving, and the R2 might actually better fit my needs.

I’m not a Tesla hater. Quite the opposite. I’ve been a fan for years. But watching Tesla walk away from the vehicle I’ve been saving for has genuinely made me question whether my next vehicle should even be a Tesla.

So I’m curious: If you were in my position, would you stick with Tesla, make the jump to Rivian, or just keep what you already have?

text:
John Stuart Mill

“But the price paid for this sort of intellectual pacification, is the sacrifice of the entire moral courage of the human mind.”

When institutions seem distant or fragile, the next moral decision is often painfully local. Being steady inside oneself does not require withdrawing care from the world. Our character is tested most sharply when nobody can promise us a predictable outcome.

Silence and reflection can help prevent other people from becoming the targets of our distress. The quotation is not a promise that trouble will disappear. It asks what sort of person we become while trouble continues. Read this passage as a challenge to examine our next response, not as a claim that any philosopher foresaw our election or that injustice is harmless.

The magical turning point begins with a single deliberate gesture rather than a victory over strangers. A rosequartz glass dragon moves through a valley of shattered bells while the wizard faces a meaningful choice. The decision is not a spectacular attack. Instead, the steady light guides a boat to shore. In the background, two differing speech circles etched onto a stone forum floor with shared middle space quietly points to freedom of thought without forced agreement.

For us, the practical beginning is smaller than the cinematic one: pause long enough to name your real concern, then offer one calm response to another person. A little restraint does not settle every argument, but it may make the next conversation possible. What does your inner life need before your next public act?

Source: On Liberty, public domain English edition

text:
judiciary possesses institutional independence. This staggered architecture prevents the entire government from moving in one direction at the same instant. The nation is given both momentum and resistance.

Equilibrium among the three branches

Constitutional equilibrium should not be confused with equal power in every matter. The branches are not symmetrical. They are functionally distinct.

The legislative branch** makes general rules, controls appropriations, represents political constituencies, and conducts oversight.
The executive branch** administers law, directs foreign and domestic policy within its authority, and provides the decisiveness necessary for government.
The judicial branch** resolves legal controversies and determines whether governmental conduct conforms to higher law.

The equilibrium emerges from interaction. Congress may enact legislation, but the president may veto it. The president may execute policy, but Congress may limit funding or conduct oversight. Congress and the president may produce a law, but courts may invalidate it if it violates the Constitution. Judicial review permits federal courts to examine governmental action and declare legislative or executive acts unconstitutional.[5] The doctrine was famously articulated in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, even though the Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “judicial review.”9

This structure is not designed to make government effortless. It is designed to make power answerable. Delay may be the price of liberty. Friction may be evidence that constitutional boundaries are operating. A government that can act quickly in every circumstance may also be a government that cannot be effectively resisted.

Judicial review and the preservation of constitutional boundaries

The Supreme Court’s role is not to settle every political disagreement. Its judicial authority is most legitimate when it translates a concrete legal controversy into a question of constitutional limits. Judicial review is therefore not a substitute for elections, nor a general license for judges to govern. It is a mechanism by which the constitutional order can adjudicate whether one branch has exceeded the authority assigned to it.

The Court’s intervention becomes especially important when ordinary political safeguards fail. If Congress is captured by the same partisan incentives as the executive, legislative oversight may weaken. If the electorate is deeply polarized, electoral correction may produce only a different form of paralysis. If fundamental rights are placed at the mercy of temporary majorities, the judiciary may be required to enforce constitutional guarantees against popular excess.

The Supreme Court itself describes judicial review as a means of ensuring that each branch recognizes the limits of its own power and of protecting rights against governmental violation.[7] This is the paradox at the heart of constitutional democracy: the majority governs, but the majority does not possess unlimited authority. The Constitution places some principles beyond the reach of ordinary political convenience.

H. L. A. Hart and the legal grammar of equilibrium

H. L. A. Hart offers a valuable philosophical vocabulary for understanding this system. Hart distinguished between primary rules, which impose duties, and secondary rules, which determine how rules are identified, changed, and adjudicated. At the center of the legal system is what he called the rule of recognition: the shared institutional criteria by which officials identify what counts as valid law.3

Applied to the American constitutional order, the rule of recognition is not merely a written sentence. It is a complex practice through which judges, legislators, administrators, and citizens recognize the authority of the Constitution, statutes, judicial decisions, elections, procedures, and institutional offices. The Constitution is the supreme legal framework; legislation must be enacted

text:
A viral chicken sandwich can bring customers through the door. It cannot guarantee lasting success. 🍗

Popeyes started in Louisiana in 1972. Its spicy chicken helped build a global franchise brand, and its 2019 chicken sandwich became a nationwide sensation.

But the latest chapter tells a tougher story.

According to Mashed, Popeyes faced declining same-store sales, growing competition and a slow response to customers demanding better value.

One major franchisee, Sailormen, filed for bankruptcy in 2026 after reporting $223 million in annual sales—and an $18 million net operating loss.

That was a franchisee bankruptcy, not the bankruptcy of the entire Popeyes brand.

The company is pursuing value offers, stronger marketing and operational upgrades to regain momentum.

My takeaway: Brand recognition gets attention. Store economics determine what owners keep.

Before buying a franchise, look beyond the logo. Understand the costs, debt, local competition and actual owner earnings.

Would you rather own a famous brand—or a less familiar business with stronger margins?

𝐋𝐎𝐔𝐈𝐒𝐈𝐀𝐍𝐀'𝐒 𝐀𝐓𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐍𝐄𝐘 𝐆𝐄𝐍𝐄𝐑𝐀𝐋 𝐁𝐋𝐎𝐂𝐊𝐄𝐃 𝟐𝟐 𝐎𝐅 𝟐𝟑 𝐈𝐍𝐍𝐎𝐂𝐄𝐍𝐂𝐄 𝐏𝐀𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐓𝐒 — 𝐄𝐋𝐕𝐈𝐒 𝐁𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐊𝐒 𝐈𝐒 𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐓𝐀𝐑𝐆𝐄𝐓

Elvis Brooks was 19 years old when prosecutors sent him to Angola for a 1977 bar s∗ooting he says he never committed. He spent the next 42 years inside the walls of one of the most violent prisons in America before a judge finally threw out his conviction. “𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘴 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴𝘯’𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦,” Brooks said of the woman now fighting to keep him from collecting a dime.

The reason he’s free at all is a cover-up. Prosecutors sat on fingerprint evidence lifted off beer cans handled by the actual gunmen — prints that did not match Brooks — for decades, until one of their own finally admitted it had been buried. 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐡𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞. Brooks’s attorney, Harry Daniels, said the state only started treating his innocence as a problem the moment he tried to collect what it owed him: “𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘰𝘯𝘭𝘺 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘥𝘦𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘦’𝘴 𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘧𝘶𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘶𝘦.”

Louisiana law says a man exonerated after decades in prison is entitled to up to $480,000. Brooks filed his claim two years ago. He still hasn’t gotten a hearing. Attorney General Liz Murrill, the state’s top lawyer, has 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝟐𝟐 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟑 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐟𝐮𝐥-𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞, insisting in her own filings against Brooks that he’s still guilty. A law professor who studies these cases didn’t mince words: “𝘐 𝘤𝘢𝘯’𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘯 𝘢𝘵𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘺 𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘨𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘷𝘦.”

This isn’t the first time Murrill has gone after an exoneree who pushed back. When one man tried to withdraw and refile his claim, she threatened to report him to the bar and block his law license unless he dropped it. Brooks says he’s not backing down either: “𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘐’𝘮 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘶𝘱, 𝘸𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘧𝘭𝘢𝘨, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘨𝘰𝘵 𝘮𝘦 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨.” He gets around New Orleans by bicycle now, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment at a senior center on a $𝟗𝟗𝟒-𝐚-𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐨𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 — the only income he has after the state took 42 years of his life and offered nothing back.

Louisiana’s own prosecutors created this mess by hiding the truth for decades. Now its attorney general is spending your tax dollars fighting the men her own state already admitted it wrongly locked up — instead of paying what they’re owed. She may win in court. But she will never undo the four decades she’s forcing an innocent 69-year-old man to relive every time he asks for what the law already says is his.

𝐋𝐨𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐚’𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐦 𝐢𝐧 𝟏𝟗𝟕𝟕. 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐲-𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞’𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥.
